facts.fact_text: The two cases concern the respondent State's alleged failure to protect the applicants' public rally from homophobic and/or transphobic acts of violence by counter-demonstrators.
The applicants relied on Article 11 of the Convention.

The applicant associations (applicants nos. 1 and 17) are Georgian non-governmental organisations set up to promote and protect the rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) people in Georgia.
The individual applicants are either staff members of the applicant associations or members and supporters of the LGBT community.

On 24 April 2013 the two applicant associations informed the Ministry of the Interior of their intention to hold a peaceful public rally on 17 May 2013 in the centre of Tbilisi to mark the International Day Against Homophobia.

On 1 May 2013 the two applicant associations informed the Ministry of the Interior of their intention to hold a peaceful public rally on 17 May 2013 in the centre of Tbilisi to mark the International Day Against Homophobia.
The planned event (the IDAHO event) would take the form of a silent twenty-minute flash mob.
The organisers of the IDAHO event indicated that the event would take place on Rustaveli Avenue, on the grounds of the former Parliament building in Tbilisi.
The organisers of the IDAHO event indicated that some fifty people would be taking part in the event.
The two applicant associations accepted the Ministry of the Interior's proposal to move the IDAHO event to Pushkin Square.
On 17 May 2013, at around 12 noon, participants in the IDAHO event started gathering at Pushkin Square.
The two cases concern the respondent State's alleged failure to protect the applicants' public rally from homophobic and/or transphobic acts of violence by counter-demonstrators.

In view of the violence committed by radical groups during a similar event held the previous year (as documented in Identoba and Others v. Georgia, no. 73235/12, §§ 10-19, 12 May 2015), the applicant associations asked the Ministry of the Interior to invest more time and energy in devising an efficient plan to protect the public rally from possible violence.
On 9 May 2013 the applicant associations informed the Ministry of the Interior of serious threats posted on the Internet by various identifiable individuals.
The threats posted on the Internet targeted the lives and health of staff members of the two applicant associations.
The threats posted on the Internet were aimed at dissuading the organisers from staging the IDAHO event.
On 13 May 2013 reports were published by various media sources that a number of ultra-conservative NGOs and clergymen were planning to hold a counter-demonstration on 17 May 2013.
On 13 May 2013 G.G. gave official notice to Tbilisi City Hall of the organising committee's intention to hold 'a prayer rally' on Rustaveli Avenue, on the grounds of the former Parliament building.

The location chosen for the 'prayer rally' (Rustaveli Avenue, on the grounds of the former Parliament building) was the same location previously chosen by the applicant associations for holding the IDAHO event.

A number of interviews with priests were published in various national newspapers in which several clergymen, including Father J., openly and repeatedly stated that the aim of the 'prayer rally' was to prevent the IDAHO event from taking place.

A number of clearly identifiable individual participants in the forthcoming counter-demonstration intensified a hate speech campaign on social media directed at the two applicant associations' staff members.
Various national newspapers and social media reported at the time that 'thousands of people' were expected to join the 'prayer rally'.
The Ministry of the Interior stated during the meetings that, according to the latest intelligence information, more than 10,000 people were planning to take part in the counter-demonstration.
On the day of the IDAHO event (17 May 2013), the Ministry of the Interior deployed some 2,000 police officers.

The 2,000 police officers deployed on 17 May 2013 were tasked with creating cordons separating Pushkin Square, where the applicants were to gather, from all the streets leading to the adjacent Rustaveli Avenue, where the 'prayer rally' was to be held.
By the early afternoon of 17 May 2013, some 35,000 to 40,000 counter-demonstrators were already gathered outside the former Parliament building.
The arriving LGBT demonstrators at Pushkin Square could see an enormous and aggressive crowd of counter-demonstrators only a few hundred metres away.
The LGBT demonstrators at Pushkin Square were separated from the counter-demonstrators only by removable metal fences and a thin cordon of unarmed and unequipped police patrol officers.
The counter-demonstrators were chanting homophobic insults and physical threats at Pushkin Square.
No riot squads could be seen at Pushkin Square on 17 May 2013.

At some point between 12.30 and 12.40 p.m. on 17 May 2013, a group of clergymen went through the police cordons to meet with senior officials from the Ministry of the Interior, including Deputy Minister G.Z.

During the negotiations, the priests urged, on behalf of the participants in the 'prayer rally', the police not to let the IDAHO event take place, arguing it would cause a clash with the counter-demonstrators.
Some of the priests can be heard on video footage repeating that 'people might get killed' during the negotiations with Ministry of the Interior officials.

A priest identified by the applicants as Father E. can be heard on video footage telling Deputy Minister G.Z. that if the police attempted to protect the participants in the IDAHO event, the clergymen would start civil disobedience and ask the Georgian army to join their side.

Video footage filmed by independent journalists shows the clergymen returning from the meeting with the Ministry of the Interior's senior officials to the counter-demonstrators' side of the police cordon.
Video footage filmed by independent journalists shows the same clergymen leading the crowd to break through the police cordon with no resistance from the police.
It appears from video footage that the participants in the IDAHO event were still in Pushkin Square when the clergymen and counter-demonstrators started passing through the police cordons.

A video-recording filmed by journalists shows a number of police officers disassembling cordons and removing metal fences that had been installed to protect the LGBT demonstrators from the counter-demonstrators.

Video footage contains scenes of police patrol officers discussing an order from the deputy head of the State Security Agency — a structural unit of the Ministry of the Interior under Deputy Minister G.Z.'s direct supervision at the material time — to remove metal fences separating Pushkin Square from Rustaveli Avenue.

Video footage shows certain police patrol officers, who were supposed to block the counter-demonstrators by standing in cordons, opening up gaps for the counter-demonstrators and saying things such as 'go!' and 'pass one by one!' as they passed through.

A video-recording shows a journalist standing in an area adjacent to Pushkin Square asking police patrol officers whether the counter-demonstrators had run over the cordon or whether it had been opened by the police, to which one of the officers replied 'it has been opened.'

Video footage shows that eventually hundreds of counter-demonstrators, led by clergymen, got through the police cordons and headed towards the group of twelve individual applicants and other participants in the IDAHO event gathered at Pushkin Square.

As the counter-demonstrators approached the scene of the IDAHO event, their behaviour became increasingly aggressive: their initial marching pace turned into a run, they yelled insults and curses, and shook wooden sticks and iron batons in their hands.
Some of the counter-demonstrators grabbed heavy stones on their way towards the group of twelve individual applicants at Pushkin Square.

Faced with the approaching mob, the group of twelve individual applicants at Pushkin Square retreated by boarding two buses that had apparently been provided by the police in advance for dispersal purposes.

Frenzied counter-demonstrators surrounded and blocked the buses containing the group of twelve individual applicants and other LGBT demonstrators, rocking the vehicles and throwing stones, wooden sticks and footstools at the windscreens.

At around 12.30 p.m. on 17 May 2013, applicants nos. 2-14, 16 and 36 (the group of fifteen individual applicants) were trying to reach the site of the IDAHO event at Pushkin Square via the narrow Vachnadze Street.
The group of fifteen individual applicants (applicants nos. 2-14, 16 and 36) were suddenly encircled by a large number of participants in the 'prayer rally' on Vachnadze Street.
The counter-demonstrators on Vachnadze Street, having identified the applicants as members of the LGBT community, started proffering homophobic insults and threats.

The number of unarmed and unequipped police officers at the scene on Vachnadze Street was insignificant in comparison to the mob and, according to the applicants, they were initially reluctant to help.

Police patrol officers near Vachnadze Street managed to remove the group of fifteen individual applicants from the mob by sneaking them into a house situated on the street and guarding its doors until a police minibus arrived.

Once the trapped activists boarded the police minibus, the counter-demonstrators, yelling 'stone them all!' and 'kill them all!', surrounded it and broke almost all the windows and the front windscreen with iron batons and stones in an attempt to pull the passengers out.

In the late afternoon of 17 May 2013, applicant no. 23, one of the twelve individual applicants who had been assaulted at Pushkin Square and removed from the scene by the police, returned to the city centre in an attempt to find out the whereabouts of some of his missing friends and colleagues.
A group of counter-demonstrators, a dozen or so people still on Rustaveli Avenue near Pushkin Square, recognised applicant no. 23 on the street in the late afternoon of 17 May 2013.
The counter-demonstrators encircled applicant no. 23 in the middle of Rustaveli Avenue and started punching and kicking him.
After finding applicant no. 23 in the basement of the supermarket, the police officers told him that, given that aggressive people were besieging the store, they could not ensure his safety.
During the beard-shaving process, the police officers made homophobic remarks and asked applicant no. 23 questions such as 'whether or not he was gay' and 'whether he had ever had sex with a woman'.

On 17 May 2013 the Ministry of the Interior launched of its own motion a general inquiry into the acts of violence committed during the clash between the participants in the IDAHO event and those in the 'prayer rally'.
Old Tbilisi Police unit no. 7 was placed in charge of the general inquiry into the acts of violence committed during the clash on 17 May 2013.
The general inquiry was conducted under Article 161 § 1 of the Criminal Code of Georgia — interference with the exercise of the right to freedom of assembly using violence.
On 9 July 2013 the general inquiry launched on 17 May 2013 was split into two separate criminal investigations.

On 25 July 2013 the two applicant associations and thirty-three of the individual applicants (not applicants nos. 20 and 24) asked the Ministry of the Interior to identify and prosecute the individuals responsible for the violence committed against them during the IDAHO event.

On 20 September 2013 the two applicant associations and thirty-three of the individual applicants (not applicants nos. 20 and 24) asked the Ministry of the Interior to identify and prosecute the individuals responsible for the violence committed against them during the IDAHO event.
The complainants enclosed a copy of the video footage concerning the incidents at Pushkin Square with their requests to the Ministry of the Interior.

The complainants requested the opening of a separate criminal investigation against the officials of the Ministry of the Interior who had been responsible for letting the counter-demonstrators pass through the police cordons and otherwise conniving in the latter's illegal actions.
No response was given by the Ministry of the Interior to the complainants' requests of 25 July and 20 September 2013.
On unspecified dates in October 2013, applicant no. 23 was interviewed by investigators from Old Tbilisi police unit no. 7 in relation to the incident on Rustaveli Avenue.
On unspecified dates in October 2013, applicant no. 36 was interviewed by investigators from Old Tbilisi police unit no. 7 in relation to the incident on Vachnadze Street.
On 6 November 2013 applicants nos. 23 and 36 enquired with the Ministry of the Interior whether any progress had been made in the investigation and whether they had been granted victim status.

On 6 November 2013 applicant no. 23 filed a criminal complaint with Old Tbilisi police unit no. 7 in which he specified the name of one of the alleged assailants of the attack on him on Rustaveli Avenue, providing the investigators with photographs and other contact details.

In his criminal complaint of 6 November 2013, applicant no. 23 asked investigators to identify the police officers whom he had accused of degrading treatment during the beard-shaving incident, providing all the details of the insults to which he was allegedly subjected.
It appears from subsequent developments in the criminal proceedings that the police never followed up on the details provided by applicant no. 23 in his criminal complaint of 6 November 2013.

On 6 November 2013 both applicant associations and all the individual applicants enquired with the Chief Public Prosecutor's Office about the progress of the investigation and whether they had been granted victim status.

On 27 December 2013 the Chief Public Prosecutor's Office responded that there were no signs of illegality in the actions of the police, who had duly discharged their duties during the demonstration by preventing grave consequences which could otherwise have occurred given the disproportionately high number of counter-demonstrators.
On 27 December 2013 the Chief Public Prosecutor's Office updated the applicants on the developments of the general inquiry launched by the Ministry of the Interior on 17 May 2013.

Following the opening of the general inquiry by the Ministry of the Interior, four counter-demonstrators were sanctioned for disorderly conduct under Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences of Georgia — a minor breach of public order — and fined 100 Georgian laris (approximately 45 euros) each.

By December 2013, criminal proceedings under Article 161 of the Criminal Code of Georgia — unlawful interference with the exercise of the right to freedom of assembly using violence, threat of violence or abusing official capacity — were pending before a trial court against four other counter-demonstrators, including a clergyman.

In April 2014, all the applicants, with the exception of applicants nos. 23 and 36, were questioned as witnesses by investigators of Old Tbilisi police unit no. 7 in relation to the incident of 17 May 2013 for the first time.

In October 2015, investigators of Old Tbilisi police unit no. 7 questioned, as witnesses, nine of its officers who had been personally involved in the security arrangements during the IDAHO event on 17 May 2013.
On 23 October 2015 the Tbilisi City Court acquitted the four accused against whom charges had been pending under Article 161 of the Criminal Code of Georgia.

The Tbilisi City Court stated that the investigation had failed to secure any evidence that would reliably prove the link between the violent dispersal of the IDAHO event and the actions of the accused on 17 May 2013.

The Tbilisi City Court identified a shortcoming in the investigation consisting of the investigators' failure to properly examine the relevant pieces of video footage of the dispersal, which the court considered crucial evidence that could have allowed for the proper identification of at least some of the perpetrators of the violent attacks.

The Tbilisi City Court identified a further shortcoming in the investigation consisting of the failure to commission a forensic examination of the buses that had been damaged by the mob during the dispersal process.
According to the material available in the case file before the Court, the second set of criminal proceedings conducted in relation to the violent clashes during the IDAHO event is still pending.
None of the applicants, except applicant no. 23, were granted victim status in the criminal proceedings related to the IDAHO event.
It is unknown whether there have been any other developments in the second set of criminal proceedings related to the IDAHO event.
